documents.text:
The recovered headset channel begins halfway through an argument about two mirror files made during Tidehaven's innings. The television ingest treated every new filename as a new occurrence, while the paper desk required a delivery signature, an umpire state and a batter transition before opening a scoring edge. Neither side reads out a replacement card. They refer instead to the early Blake packet, the Caleb-Owen interval and the wicket ownership queue as one linked reconciliation, because changing any one of those packets also changes the balance used to check the others.

The first mirror contains the movement seen while Blake and Sharp crossed. A wireless operator associates the visible crossing with Blake; the square-leg channel associates the same frame with the already registered wide. The two descriptions can each support a locally tidy opening card. Only the event headers distinguish them: the frame shares TV-001-C with the umpire-wide record, whereas Blake's later singles have separate ball-change markers. The reverse-angle cover clip is also in the mirror index, so accepting it as new would affect both Blake's personal stream and the team boundary before his catch.

A similar fork appears in the Caleb-Owen interval. One cache preserves the apparent run after Owen withdrew and treats the second wide picture as another delivery. The venue book keeps AW-11-D in the dead-ball channel and links the later wide picture to its earlier signal. The interval can be made to balance under either cache if its start boundary is copied from the same cache; it cannot be reconciled against the independently sealed wicket state and the innings-wide signatures under both. This is why the headset staff refuse to repair Owen, the stand and the extras sheet one row at a time.

The wicket ownership queue creates a third dependency. A production continuation places Theo's catch beside Wells, but the spell-transition header names Elias. Moving that edge affects Wells's bowling partition while the team dismissal remains. The clerk checks the early Vance signatures, the Wells terminal delivery and the Elias transition together, rather than accepting a compact bowler total from the television rundown. The replay filenames for Nolan, Owen and Dylan are mirror nodes and never create new fallen-batter transitions.

During the chase the two systems diverge again. One branch keeps the airborne Finch picture as Owen's dismissal and treats the later Ben catch as a replay; the other attaches the opening picture to the umpire's overstep and keeps OM-02-F as the live dismissal. Both branches contain one dramatic catch and can look plausible in isolation. The incoming-batter marker, the fifth counted delivery in Owen's second over and the no-ball card do not agree with the first branch when considered together.

The Finch ledger cannot be closed at that point because the downstream feed has also copied his opening cover boundary into the Noah partnership. A different late ball, CF-04-A, has an overstep marker and a completed run from Finch's bat. If the copied boundary is kept while the overstep packet is discarded, the broadcast reaches a locally plausible winning picture but disagrees with the paper legal-ball sequence. If the live packet is kept and the mirror edge is collapsed, batter ownership, no-ball class, partnership progression and the terminal chase state move together.

The registry closure note defines authority without publishing target values. Umpire event states govern legality and extras class. Paper scoring governs batter and partnership ownership only after those event states are attached. Production captions and replay filenames may supply identity evidence but cannot create a delivery, wicket or run by themselves. A candidate state is rejected if one event signature is consumed twice or if a mirror node advances a wicket or legal-ball boundary.

For Tidehaven the closure test is performed on one connected component containing TV-001-C, AW-11-D, the Wells-Elias spell transition, the fifth-wicket boundary and the terminal legal-ball state. The accepted component must conserve the innings between batter and extras ledgers, preserve ten distinct dismissals, and place each bowler-credited wicket on a live delivery. Removing any one of those checks leaves both cache interpretations usable; applying all of them leaves one.

For Ridgefield the connected component contains the opening overstep, OM-02-F, the replayed Finch boundary, CF-04-A and the final counted delivery. It must preserve the opening-stand wicket boundary, the second-stand start, the accepted no-ball identities and the target relationship to Tidehaven. The winning packet cannot be chosen independently of Finch's innings line or Owen's bowling line. The final signature set is signed, but no compact score row is transmitted on this channel.

Brookhaven's synchronization memorandum was written because the venue board and the ingestion service produced two internally balanced first-innings cards. The discrepancy is not confined to one field. It passes through Elena's opening attribution, the leg-bye class, the duplicated free-hit frame, the Rowan-Nora partnership and the fourth-wicket boundary. The memorandum keeps both reconstructions open while it traces their event signatures.

The opening pad picture is the first fork. One reconstruction attaches the visible run to Elena because she is striker; the other follows the delayed square-leg signal and puts the event outside the bat. Mira's opening contribution and the partnership boundary are independently fixed, but the local television ribbon can be balanced under either ownership choice. The delayed card has the same delivery fingerprint as the ringed pad event and a different fingerprint from Elena's cover drive.

The long Rowan-Nora association contains a second fork. The free-hit setup was written twice by the ingestion service. One worksheet row has the live legal-transition signature and one has only the copied picture. A provisional branch preserves both rows, raises the non-batter stream and shifts the boundary at Rowan's dismissal. Another branch collapses the copied frame. Nora's personal feed also carries the disputed item, so adjusting only partnership extras creates a second inconsistency rather than resolving the first.

The wicket partition must be solved with the same component. Aila's early delivery signatures establish two genuine transitions, while the Mira lbw is owned by Nia's end log. Celeste's line contains delivered dismissals separated by Lena's run out, which remains a team wicket without a bowling credit. A production summary can swap one ownership edge and still show eight fallen batters; it fails only when delivery owners and the non-bowler dismissal are checked together.

The chase has its own connected fork. A cached Sinclair caption is attached to Aila's old stump clip, while later live Sinclair deliveries dismiss different batters. Separately, the Sienna association carries a copied wide picture and Emilia's provisional batter feed carries the same unit. The Ruth association later receives another replay with an old fingerprint. A row-by-row repair can make Jade's bowling line, Emilia's innings line or either partnership look plausible, but not all of them against the accepted wide signatures and wicket transitions.

No final number is supplied in the memorandum. It records that the chase-wide signatures are distributed across the opening, Sienna, Celeste, Ruth and closing passages; only packets with an umpire call and a legal-transition position enter the class. The Sienna and Ruth replay packets are retained as evidence links, not scoring nodes. Emilia's component therefore has to be reconstructed across nonadjacent partnerships rather than copied from either television profile.

The arbitration ruling states three tests. First, a graphics row without a legal transition cannot survive as a new delivery. Second, a run-out changes batter, partnership and team-wicket state but cannot be reassigned to a bowler. Third, the same event fingerprint cannot occupy both a batter component and an extras component. The ruling identifies the opening pad card, the free-hit mirror pair and the stale Sinclair caption by signature but does not print their numeric effects.

The first-innings candidate must satisfy batter-plus-extras conservation, the sealed Rowan dismissal boundary, eight distinct fallen-batter events and the bowling-credit partition. Each test alone permits the venue branch or the ingestion branch after a compensating local edit. Their intersection does not. The chase candidate must satisfy the accepted wide-signature set, the Sienna and Ruth partnership boundaries, Emilia's cross-partnership ownership and the dismissal-owner registry. The signed registry stores only the surviving event edges.

The engineering review treats the Shoreline innings as two synchronized streams rather than a sequence of independent card rows. The first stream begins with Finn's opening pad contact and continues through the Carter boundary. The second begins with Dylan's duplicated running packet and continues through the wide reconnect and the Benton-Zane ownership split. Either stream can be patched locally; the combined innings cannot accept both local patches.

The opening pad contact is visible on the striker camera, so the television branch assigns it to Finn. The umpire branch links the same delivery signature to the leg-bye signal. Because the team score advances under either interpretation, the disagreement survives the opening partnership and Rory's scoreless stay. It becomes consequential only when Finn's cross-partnership batter components, the Finn-Carter boundary and the innings extras classes are conserved together.

The Carter stand contains a second packet that the boundary camera places after Carter's dismissal signature. A venue branch keeps it within the stand because the pictures are contiguous; the event branch attaches it to the following association. Each branch can produce a coherent local partnership ribbon by choosing the matching upper boundary. Only the independently sealed third-wicket state and the delivery transition decide which boundary is permitted.

Dylan's running event creates the same kind of coupled ambiguity. The automatic packet and the live scoring record share a running signature. Keeping both shifts Dylan's innings line and the downstream team states; collapsing the mirror changes the Connor and Evan windows used to reconstruct him. The reconnect wide packet and the accepted bowler-wide cards supply a separate conservation channel, so a compensating edit to Dylan alone does not close the innings.

Bowling ownership is deliberately not summarized. A surname-only Miles caption can refer to Carter the batter, Benton the bowler or Aaron in the later chase. The registry attaches credits only when a live delivery signature, dismissed batter and incoming-batter transition agree. Alternate camera angles for the Zane and Benton dismissals remain mirror nodes. This partition is checked against ten distinct first-innings dismissals rather than a television wicket numeral.

In the chase, the Carter-Arin feed opens one live wide and one automatic packet. A player-profile branch consumes both and lowers the remaining extras needed elsewhere; the authority branch merges the packet with the live call. Tyler's later pad event then determines whether a unit stays with his bat or enters a non-batter channel. Both choices can be made to fit a short local partnership graphic, but they cannot both satisfy Arin's cross-window account, Tyler's later contribution, the accepted chase-wide signatures and the third-wicket boundary.

Aaron's bowling cache is part of that same component. Tyler and Blake have distinct live dismissal signatures, Leo's slow motion is a mirror of his live ball, and Cameron's stumping propagates a bowler credit from a legal delivery. A cache that counts the mirror but misses the stumping reaches a plausible local total. It fails the owner registry even though the numeral happens to balance. The review therefore closes event edges, not bowler rows.

The terminal register supplies no completed scorecard. For Shoreline it preserves the legal closing position, the third-wicket event boundary, the accepted extras categories and a one-owner rule for every fallen batter. An admissible state must use one edge for each live scoring or dismissal event, may use mirror clips only as evidence, and must conserve batter and extras streams against the terminal state. Dropping any one rule leaves both engineering patches feasible.

For Meridian the register preserves the first- and second-wicket boundaries, the fourth legitimate ball of Connor's over for the third wicket, the terminal legal-ball position and the accepted source hierarchy. It requires the Carter-Arin packet, Tyler pad attribution and Aaron stumping propagation to be solved together. The player profile, television ribbon and bowling cache are provisional views; the delivery authority and terminal registry control the surviving graph.
